newsitem.title: USA: Bernard Ebbers leads WorldCom to the big time.
newsitem.headline: Bernard Ebbers leads WorldCom to the big time.

text.p: Three times a college drop-out, Bernard Ebbers is one of the unlikeliest candidates to join the big league of telecommunications entreprenuers, but even his detractors would admit that he did it with style.

Ebbers' WorldCom Inc. has pursued an insatiable diet of acquisitions since its formation as LDDS in 1983, and on Monday agreed to a $14 billion acquisition of MFS Communications Co. Inc., which offers local telephone services to businesses.

That takeover, Ebbers's 40th since Worldcom was founded, will make WorldCom comparable in market value to MCI Communications Corp. or Sprint Corp., the numbers two and three in the long distance telephone business, and as big as some regional Bells.

"I never have thought I want to do this because I want to be bigger than so and so. The point is, it puts more value in my shares. I'm selfish that way," the tall, bearded Ebbers told Reuters in an interview on Monday.

Being selfish has made others rich too. WorldCom was the best performing stock over 10 years of more than 1,000 surveyed by the Wall Street Journal earlier this year, with an average annual gain of 57 percent a year.

Worldcom has come a long way since Ebbers and a group of business associates met in a coffee shop in Hattiesburg, Miss., in September 1983 -- a month after Judge Harold Greene ordered the final break-up of Ma Bell -- and founded LDDS, its name suggested by a waitress there.

Ebbers, fond of smoking fat cigars long before they came back into fashion, has also cultivated a slow-sounding southern demeanor that made many, particularly in fast-talking Wall Street, underestimate him.
But Ebbers is fast when opportunity beckons.

James Crowe, chairman and chief executive of MFS recalled that the first meeting to size up the two busineses took place on August 13, the day after MFS finalised its own $2 billion takeover of internet service provider UUNET.
"I thought it was going to be an introductory meeting," Crowe told Reuters. But within an hour a broad outline for merging the two companies had been agreed.
Born in Edmonton, Alberta, Ebbers came to Mississippi on a basketball scholarship.
He began his first business in 1974, a motel-restaurant in Columbia, Miss. and has always made shareholder value the keystone of his philosophy.
But now he may have crossed an important rubicon because for the first time the MFS buy is expected to dilute earnings before growth resumes at a faster pace.

"WorldCom has traditionally been very focused on earnings, price earnings multiples and anti-dilutive deals. They have crossed a very significant barrier here," said Robert McNamara, a mergers and acquisitions advisor at consultants Broadview Associates.
Nevertheless, analysts are unanimous Ebbers has what it takes to see where the industry is going and profit from it.
And if a regional Bell decides that now is the last chance to buy a fast growing business like WorldCom and break-up the MFS takeover, Ebbers will still be laughing.
His 14 million WorldCom shares will be worth even more than their current $44 million.
